work-organization.text: Reeling joined trained handwork with machinery; sericulture, teaching and cold storage solved different practical problems. Learning could spread while the conditions and protection of workers remained unequal and source-specific.

production.text: Imported machinery worked within local farming, training and construction networks.

evidence.text: Industrial heritage documents a production system more directly than every worker’s experience.

name: Tomioka: adapting an industrial system
geographicPrecision: Mill-site locator within a regional production system.

interval.label: Model mill opened October 1872
interval.note: Opening event; the mill and associated techniques continued afterward. This is not an endpoint for Japanese industrialization.

question: What does it take to move a technology between places?
summary: Tomioka’s imported machinery depended on trained women, local building work and people raising silkworms. Later teaching, adaptation and storage extended the inquiry beyond the model mill; evidence of working conditions and legal protection needs its own dates and places.

sections.title: A machine still needs practiced hands
sections.text: When the government mill opened in October 1872, machinery arrived within an existing silk-producing region. Japanese carpenters constructed buildings that joined French design with local timber, brick and plaster work. Inside, women learned demanding operations. Sashinami describes sorting cocoons, finding and drawing their filaments from hot water, joining them into raw silk and winding at the speed of powered machinery. Reliable output depended on attention and practice. A reel could organize motion without making the worker’s judgment unnecessary. French instructors and Japanese women trained by them helped others acquire these skills.

citations.locator: Tomioka Silk Mill; Women Mill Workers

sections.title: Workers carried knowledge elsewhere
sections.text: One learner became a teacher. The National Diet Library records Wada Ei(ko) at Tomioka from April 1873 to July 1874, followed by instruction at another mill and, in 1878, a prefectural appointment. Her career makes women active participants in moving techniques. At the separate Rokkōsha mill in Matsushiro, imported arrangements were reworked using local materials. Nakamura and Molteni explain how other mills also replaced expensive components and combined different technical models. Adaptation involved decisions about construction, power and handling, rather than simply copying a complete French factory. Wada’s remembered comparison was written much later.

sections.title: The crop has its own timetable
sections.text: Silk work also depended on keeping silkworms alive and producing cocoons. The region’s farmhouse experiments managed airflow, warmth and humidity. Takayama-sha became a school in 1884, joining teaching with practical rearing. Arafune’s first cold-storage units began operating in 1905. Cooling delayed eggs hatching; marked cards, testing, labels and catalogues helped organize storage and return. Such work changed when a living crop could be raised. The four heritage components therefore explain connected functions with different beginnings. They are not four parts opened together in 1872, nor proof of one recovered shipment between them.

sections.title: Training and protection are different questions
sections.text: Learning a valuable skill did not settle who controlled working time. Tomioka’s institutional account describes dormitories and trainers. Broader evidence from Suwa concerns other workplaces and must stay located there. The Factory Act was promulgated in 1911 but implemented only in September 1916. Its initial scope and exceptions matter when asking what protection meant in practice. Buildings, production and a model institution’s aims cannot alone tell us whether every worker could rest, leave or benefit equally.

claims.text: The mill opened in October 1872, combining French technical input with Japanese construction and regional silk expertise.
claims.checkedBy: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval

returnPrompt: What local skills would a newly imported machine still depend on?

deeperReading.title: A recollection has more than one date
deeperReading.text: Wada’s experience and its publication are separate evidence. The NDL says that she began writing memories in 1907; an edited book appeared in 1931. Nakamura and Molteni’s 1994 English chapter quotes a later Japanese edition when discussing her visit to Rokkōsha. Their chapter calls her Wada Hide, while the NDL uses Ei(ko). Here the biographical and technical accounts remain attributed to their sources. The original Japanese memoir and those editions have not been independently read or translated. The comparison shows what one remembered about adapting materials, without becoming a contemporary inspection of every reel.

deeperReading.title: Implementation is not a completed outcome
deeperReading.text: The National Archives separates the 1911 law from its 1916 implementation. Nakamura and Molteni describe provisions allowing extended hours in silk-reeling. They also mediate a woman’s recollection of long days at an Okaya mill in 1917, the year after implementation. Their note leads to a 1981 publication; that original interview volume was not read here. The factory-inspection annual they cite is another record, not this woman’s own speech. Together these materials make a useful question: what happened after a rule existed? They do not supply a complete compliance history for Tomioka or speak for every worker. A model mill, a law and a worker’s retrospective account each require a different kind of interpretation.

evidenceReading.title: Hands, memories and rules
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected passages. A training account, a later recollection and an institutional legal caption answer different questions.

items.label: Technical skill is part of production
items.text: Sashinami’s exposed introduction describes women learning to sort cocoons, join filaments and reel at machine speed, then teaching other women.
items.interpretation: Machinery and human practice worked together. The passage does not count every trainee, recover each woman’s consent or establish every factory’s conditions.

items.label: A memory can explain a comparison
items.text: The NDL dates Wada’s Tomioka employment to 1873–74 and her memory-writing from 1907. The 1994 chapter uses her later account when comparing materials at Rokkōsha.
items.interpretation: Experience, remembering, editing and translation have different dates. The original Japanese memoir was not freshly read, and Rokkōsha’s equipment is not silently transferred to Tomioka.

items.label: A law needs an implementation history
items.text: The National Archives gives 1911 promulgation and September 1916 implementation. The labor chapter discusses exceptions and a later recollection of long working days at Okaya.
items.interpretation: The legal dates establish different steps. The recollection supplies a particular remembered experience through a later publication, rather than proving uniform compliance or violation at every mill.

familyActivity.title: What would a machine still need?
steps: Use the supplied capsule to name three jobs: tending silkworms, reeling silk and keeping egg cards in cool storage. Explain why one machine could not do all three.

If the contemporary mill print is included, find two rows of people and equipment, and the roof supports. Describe what is drawn. If it is not available, use the capsule’s description of those features.
Make date cards for 1872, 1884 and 1905. Match the mill, school and cold storage to them. Explain why the school and storage cannot be things opened with the mill in 1872.

Sort two questions: What arrangement does the artist show? Could every worker leave or rest when she wanted? Decide which needs more evidence, then return to the opening question about moving technology.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: Tomioka opened in October 1872. Reeling required women to handle filaments and learn machine-paced work; other tasks included raising silkworms. Takayama-sha became a practical sericulture school in 1884, and Arafune’s first cold-storage units operated in 1905. Cooling helped delay hatching, while labels and catalogues organized egg cards. The NDL’s contemporary interior print arranges workers and equipment in two receding rows beneath roof supports. It is an artist’s published representation, not a photograph, payroll or complete account of freedom and rest. The NDL brackets its impression [1872]; MAFF dates a comparable impression 1873. The date match is mill/1872, school/1884, storage/1905. The image can support observations about its drawn arrangement; questions about workers’ choices require appropriate records and attributed accounts.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian, worker/community or family approval
review.scope: Selected positive explanation of training, adaptation, regional sericulture/storage and the distinction between legislation and implementation. Two inherited source scopes renewed with their prior dated consultation retained; eight new selected source records. The complete exact opening interval, identity, original claim and dimensions remain unchanged. The reference frame reaches 1916 and distinguishes later recollection/publication. The local place study uses four published modern UNESCO reference points; source plans and shipment routes are not reproduced. The included NDL print extends the originally empty object list; its bracketed catalogue attribution, rights status and unknown modern digitization date remain distinct.
limitations: The original Japanese Wada memoir, 1931/1978 editions, 1981 Okaya interview volume, 1903 surveys, original Factory Act and inspection annual were not read. English reminiscences are mediated through identified scholarship; the institutional Japanese legal caption is editorially paraphrased, not an independent statute translation.

The 2022 chapter was read only at its exposed Introduction/Summary and metadata; the complete chapter and figure were unavailable in this consultation. The 1994 source was read at selected HTML passages, not as a fresh complete book, original experiment or universal workforce census. Suwa, Okaya and Matsushiro evidence is not a Tomioka payroll or recovered equipment list.

The included NDL print is an artistic representation with bracketed [1872] catalogue attribution; a comparable MAFF impression is dated 1873. Their exact copy/state relationship and the modern scan/exposure dates remain unverified. The MAFF image is research-only. No individual identity, exact shift, measured room plan, universal working conditions or new guide is inferred from the NDL image. Public-domain PDM status is separate from NDL’s expressly stated reproduction terms and required source credit.

UNESCO coordinates identify modern component-reference points to the displayed second. The older/current Tajima difference is retained explicitly; no historical border, route, workstation or particular batch connection inferred. The large nomination, linked map and full heritage-management documentation were not consulted.

Internal author checking does not establish independent historian approval, real adult/family usability, human screen-reader behavior, physical-device or print quality. No historical worker/community assent or modern partner endorsement is represented.

placeStudy.title: Four places with different jobs and dates
placeStudy.description: Published UNESCO component-reference points, displayed to the source table’s nearest second, orient a regional inquiry. The mill, farmhouse, school and cold-storage site had different histories. Points are modern property locators, not historical workstations or proof that a particular batch traveled between them. No shipment route, border or reconstructed site plan is drawn. The original case locator is preserved separately.

points.label: Tomioka Silk Mill
points.text: UNESCO 1449-001: E138°53′16″, N36°15′19″. The government mill opened in October 1872. This property-reference point does not identify an individual reel or worker.

points.label: Tajima Yahei Sericulture Farm
points.text: UNESCO 1449-002: E139°14′21″, N36°14′48″. The current table’s point is used explicitly; an older nomination search excerpt differs by one second in each coordinate. The 1863 farmhouse’s ventilation belongs to a history earlier than the model mill.

points.label: Takayama-sha Sericulture School
points.text: UNESCO 1449-003: E139°1′54″, N36°12′12″. The farm became a school in 1884. Learning to manage warmth, airflow and humidity supported raising silkworms; it was a different task from reeling.

points.label: Arafune Cold Storage
points.text: UNESCO 1449-004: E138°38′7″, N36°14′48″. The first units operated in 1905. Cooling postponed hatching; labels and catalogues supported returning egg cards when needed. This locator does not establish a particular delivery route.
